subject.title: Marthe Lonely
subject.author: Kenneth Rexroth
subject.text:
m

MARTHE LONELY
To think of you surcharged with
Loneliness. To hear your voice
Over the recorder say,
"Loneliness." The word, the voice,
So full of it, and I, with
You away, so lost in it-
Lost in loneliness and pain,
Black and unendurable,
Thinking of you with every
Corpuscle of my flesh, in
Every instant of night
And day. O, my love, the times
We have forgotten love, and
Sat lonely beside each other.
We have eaten together,
Lonely behind our plates, we
Have hidden behind children,
We have slept together in
A lonely bed. Now my heart
Turns towards you, awake at last,
Penitent, lost in the last
Loneliness. Speak to me. Talk
To me. Break the black silence.
Speak of a tree full of leaves,
Of a flying bird, the new
Moon in the sunset, a poem,
A book, a person-all the
Casual healing speech
Of your resonant, quiet voice.
The word freedom. The word peace.

title: He Begged Her to Speak. She Left Instead.
standfirst: In 1956 Kenneth Rexroth published a sequence asking his wife's recorded voice to cure his loneliness. The same year, by every account of the marriage, she was already falling for another poet — and already choosing to leave quietly rather than explain.

sections.heading: A Word Rexroth Will Not Put Down
sections.body: Count one word and "Marthe Lonely" comes apart in your hands: loneliness, or its plainer form lonely, turns up seven times across thirty short lines, plus once more in the title. Nothing else in the poem gets close. That is strange from a poet whose other work favors hard, specific nouns — a camping trip high on a ridge, a macaroni dinner eaten by lamplight, starlight picked out through a telescope — the kind of plain, observed detail that runs through the nature poems [Rexroth read aloud](https://ojs.lib.uwo.ca/index.php/esc/article/download/9883/7983/) on his own weekly radio program. Almost none of that survives here. The only concrete things he actually names are the things he is begging someone else to supply instead: a tree full of leaves, a flying bird, the new moon in the sunset. Everything that is his to say stays abstract — pain, love, freedom, peace — right down to the one startling exception, where devotion turns almost clinical: he is thinking of her "with every / Corpuscle of my flesh," a word for a blood cell standing in for a heart.

sections.heading: A Marriage That Took Nine Years to Become Legal
sections.body: Marthe Larsen was a philosophy student at Berkeley when she met Rexroth, twenty years her senior, according to [The Marthe Project](https://www.themartheproject.org/marthe-whitcomb). In 1949 the two travelled to France and married in [Aix-en-Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aix-en-Provence) — a wedding one biographical reference [flatly calls bigamy](https://www.nndb.com/people/198/000049051/), since Rexroth's previous marriage, to the nurse Marie Kass, had not yet been dissolved. Exactly when it was dissolved is contested: that same source dates the Kass divorce to 1955, while [EBSCO's](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/kenneth-rexroth/) and [Encyclopedia.com's](https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/culture-magazines/rexroth-kenneth-1905-1982) reference entries both put it in 1948 — a year before the Aix wedding, which would make the charge of bigamy hard to sustain. What no source disputes is the eventual fix: Rexroth and Larsen were not married in a form the state recognized until 1958, two years after "Seven Poems for Marthe, My Wife" went to print. Their daughters, Mary and Katharine, were born in 1950 and 1954, into a marriage that, on paper, barely existed yet.

sections.heading: The Recorder Already Had a Job
sections.body: The recorder in "Marthe Lonely" is not a literary flourish. Rexroth [helped found](https://ojs.lib.uwo.ca/index.php/esc/article/download/9883/7983/) KPFA, the country's first listener-sponsored FM station, in 1949, and for roughly twenty years after that he hosted its weekly book-review program, "Books." According to Brook Houglum's study of that broadcast work, Rexroth wrote the show, his autobiographical novel, and several essays the same way: by speaking directly into a tape recorder at home and having the results transcribed, in order to "preserve the spontaneous, oral character of the style." In the preface to his autobiography he put it more plainly: "I have spent my life striving to write the way I talk." The machine this poem turns to for a lost voice was, in that house, already doing the opposite job daily — turning Rexroth's own spoken voice into print and broadcast. Houglum's essay also records that on 13 January 1957, a little over three months after "Seven Poems for Marthe, My Wife" ran in Poetry, Rexroth read several of its poems aloud on "Books" — carrying a sequence built around one recorded voice back out through the same kind of machine, to every listener KPFA had.

sections.heading: The Other Poet Already in the House
sections.body: In the spring of 1956 — the same year "Seven Poems for Marthe, My Wife" went to print — [Robert Creeley visited San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Creeley) for two months and met Allen Ginsberg, who had recently completed "Howl." Marthe helped Creeley find work; he later recalled simply that "[Martha Rexroth gave me the job as I remember](https://allenginsberg.org/2017/05/saturday-may-20-robert-creeley/)." One of the jobs was typing up a mimeograph edition of "Howl," twenty-five copies, ahead of the poem's wider publication. Creeley typed it; Marthe ran the copies off herself. A special-collections account of one surviving copy, held at Dartmouth, describes the edition bluntly as ["typed by poet Robert Creeley and run off by Kenneth Rexroth's wife (and Creeley's lover), Marthe"](https://raunerlibrary.blogspot.com/2011/12/i-saw-best-minds-of-my-generation.html). The Marthe Project, which preserves her own later testimony about the marriage, puts the same fact more gently — that she fell in love with Creeley [as her marriage to Rexroth deteriorated](https://www.themartheproject.org/marthe-whitcomb) — but the timeline does not move. The poem asking her to cure a loneliness with her voice, and the mimeograph she ran off for the man she was falling for, belong to the same few months.

sections.heading: A Name Replaced by a Pronoun
sections.body: Rexroth and Larsen's marriage, legalized only in 1958, ended in divorce in 1961 — a date every source consulted here agrees on. What happened to the poems afterward is less settled. One account of the breakup says Rexroth "[tried to expurgate mention of her from all of his poetry](https://patrickmurfin.blogspot.com/2014/04/national-poetry-monthdaddy-to-beats.html)" once Marthe left; a later defender of his reputation, reviewing a biography that reads the same fact as duplicity, confirms the substance of it while rejecting the motive, writing that Rexroth simply [replaced Marthe's name with "she"](https://www.bopsecrets.org/rexroth/solt-hamalian.htm) when he reprinted the love poems. Either way, what is left of a devotion once addressed directly to "Marthe" survives mostly under a pronoun now. The mimeograph she ran off that same year had the opposite fate: one surviving copy, mailed with a long explanatory letter to the critic Richard Eberhart, helped prompt the [New York Times piece credited with launching the Beat Generation](https://raunerlibrary.blogspot.com/2011/12/i-saw-best-minds-of-my-generation.html) into wider American culture. The poem asked her, seven times over, to break a silence. She broke it in the other direction — not explaining, just leaving — and what remains of her side of that year is thinner than what remains of the typescript she ran off a mimeograph machine to help someone else become famous.
